paras.text: Argument Architecture & Conditional Logic, Audio Lecture

This is the chapter every later chapter in this track assumes you already know. Before you can spot a flawed strengthen question, a sloppy necessary assumption, or a sales pitch leaning on a reversed conditional, you have to know how to take an argument apart into its actual pieces, and you have to know exactly which if-then rewrites are guaranteed and which ones are traps. Nothing here is an opinion. It is formal logic, true the same way a definition is true, and the only real danger in this whole subject is translating a sentence backwards without noticing.

Let me start with the single most useful sentence in this entire track, because everything else is really just this one idea applied five different ways. A conditional statement, an if-then statement, makes exactly one promise. If A, then B means that whenever A is true, B is true. It says absolutely nothing about what happens when A is false. Nothing. Hold onto that, because every trap coming up is someone quietly forgetting it.
Idea one. What an argument actually is.

An argument, in this sense, is not a fight, it is a claim plus the reasons given for it. The claim is the conclusion. The reasons are the premises. A sentence sitting there with no reason attached is just an assertion, it is not an argument at all.

You find the pieces fast with indicator words. Premise indicators, words that tell you a reason is coming, are since, because, given that, for, as, in light of, after all. Conclusion indicators, words that tell you the main point is coming, are therefore, thus, so, hence, it follows that, consequently, which means.

Here is a restoration example. Since the moisture meter read above seventeen percent on three separate studs, and since Category 2 water sat in that wall cavity for more than forty eight hours, the drywall and insulation in that section must be removed. Two premises, both flagged by the word since. One conclusion, that the materials must be removed.

Now here is the part people get backwards constantly. The conclusion is not whatever sentence happens to come last. It is whatever the other statements are trying to establish, and it can sit first, last, or buried in the middle. If I flip that restoration sentence around and put the conclusion first, nothing about the actual logical structure changes.

And plenty of real arguments drop the indicator words entirely, on purpose, especially in sales pitches, because the writer wants the leap from reason to conclusion to feel automatic instead of argued for. This contractor replaced forty roofs last year, he's the right guy for your job. No since, no therefore. The test for whether that is still an argument: try inserting the word therefore between the two sentences. It fits, so it is an argument, just an undressed one.

Question for you. Go back to the roofing sentence I just gave you, forty roofs last year, he's the right guy. Name the premise and the conclusion out loud, and tell me what test you used to confirm it was actually an argument.
Premise: he replaced forty roofs last year. Conclusion: he's the right guy for the job. The test was inserting the word therefore between the two sentences and checking the meaning still held.
Idea two. The assumption gap.

Almost no real argument states every single thing it actually needs to reach its conclusion. The assumption gap is whatever the conclusion silently depends on that was never written down. You find it by asking what would have to be true for the stated premises to actually get you all the way to the conclusion, and then checking whether that thing was ever said out loud.

Claims example. A denial letter says the policy requires prompt notice, the insured waited eleven months, therefore the claim is properly denied. Both stated facts can be completely true. The unstated assumption doing all the actual work is that eleven months definitely fails to count as prompt notice under this specific policy's wording, with nothing, no discovery rule, no waiver, excusing it. The letter never proves that, it just writes the conclusion as if the gap were already closed.

Sales example, and this one is almost funny once you see it. Our dehumidifiers run around the clock in your basement, so your mold risk is zero. The premise is true, the machine really does run constantly. The assumption carrying the whole conclusion is that nonstop dehumidification is, by itself, enough to erase mold risk completely, no role for ventilation, no role for moisture already behind a wall. Say that assumption out loud and it is obviously too big for the fact pattern to support.

This is the most useful habit in the whole domain, by the way. Turning a vague feeling that something is off into a specific, nameable, testable sentence. That is the entire difference between sounding smart in an argument and actually winning one.
Idea three. The basic conditional, and the one move that is always safe.

If A, then B. A is the antecedent, the if part. B is the consequent, the then part. Given that statement, there is exactly one automatic, guaranteed, always-valid rewrite, and it is called the contrapositive. If not B, then not A.

Test it against something real. If the water intrusion is Category 3, contaminated water, then all porous materials in that area must be removed. Contrapositive: if the porous materials do not have to be removed, then the water was not Category 3. Walk that through in your head. If removal had genuinely been required, it would only be because of Category 3 water, per the rule, so no required removal means the water was not Category 3. It holds, every time, guaranteed.
Idea four. The converse and the inverse, and why they feel just as natural and are both wrong.
Given if A, then B, the converse is if B, then A. It is not equivalent. The original statement never promises anything about it.

Same Category 3 example. Converse: if porous materials must be removed, then the water was Category 3. Does that hold? No. A slow, boring Category 1 leak that sat for three weeks and grew mold can also force removal, with zero contaminated water anywhere near it. Removal being required proves nothing about the water category.

The inverse is if not A, then not B, and it is logically identical to the converse's contrapositive, so if you fall for one you are exposed to the other. If the water is not Category 3, then removal is not required. Same counterexample kills it. The slow leak with mold growth still forces removal, no Category 3 water involved.

Here is the sales version of this trap, because it is everywhere in a closing script. If you sign today, you lock in this price. A homeowner hears that and slides, almost without noticing, into so if I want to lock in the price, I have to sign today. That is the converse, assumed true with zero justification. The original sentence never said signing today was the only way to the same price.

Question for you. I will give you a conditional, and I want you to say the contrapositive, and then tell me whether the converse would hold. If a loss is excluded under the policy, the carrier does not owe payment.

Contrapositive: if the carrier owes payment, the loss was not excluded. That one holds, it is guaranteed. The converse would be, if the loss was not excluded, the carrier owes payment, and that one does not automatically hold, because plenty of non-excluded losses could still fail for other reasons, like a coverage limit already exhausted or a condition not yet satisfied.
Idea five. Translating the four everyday phrases, and this is where the money is.

Four phrases each translate into an if-then statement, and two of the four run in the direction almost everybody guesses wrong. Do not memorize a pattern here. Test every single one against a real substitution, the way I am about to show you, because pattern matching the English phrase is exactly how this goes backwards.

A only if B translates to if A, then B. Test: we will start mold remediation only if the moisture meter reads below fifteen percent. A is we start remediation, B is the meter reads below fifteen. Rule says A implies B. Check it: remediation only ever starts once the threshold clears, so remediation actually happening proves the threshold was already met. It matches.

Unless A, B translates to if not A, then B. Test: unless the insured gives timely notice, the claim is barred. A is gives timely notice, B is claim is barred. Rule says not A implies B. Check it: the absence of timely notice is exactly what triggers the bar. It matches.

A is necessary for B translates to if B, then A. Test: being on the active roster is necessary for a player to score fantasy points. A is active roster, B is scores points. Rule says B implies A. Check it: a player can be active and score zero, so A does not guarantee B, but scoring any points absolutely requires having been active, so B does guarantee A. It matches, in that one direction only.

A is sufficient for B translates to if A, then B. Test: signing today is sufficient to lock in this price. A is sign today, B is price locked. Rule says A implies B. Check it: that is exactly the promise made, nothing more, and it says nothing about whether signing today is the only way to the same price.

Notice what just happened. Necessary for and sufficient for sound like mirror images of the same idea, and they point in completely opposite directions. Necessary for puts B first. Sufficient for puts A first. The only reliable way through this under time pressure is the substitution test you just watched four times in a row, not a memorized rule of thumb.

One more pair, because it reverses only if. Plain A if B translates to if B, then A, not if A, then B. Plain if marks a sufficient condition for the thing stated first. Only if marks a necessary condition for it. Swap one word for the other in the same sentence and you flip the entire arrow.

Question for you. A contract clause says the warranty is honored if the homeowner keeps the gutters cleaned annually. Tell me the correct translation, and tell me whether skipping the cleaning proves the warranty is void.

Plain if, so it translates to if B, then A: if the gutters are cleaned, the warranty is honored. Cleaning is sufficient for the warranty, not necessary for it, since that would require only if. So skipping the cleaning does not, by this clause alone, prove the warranty is void.
Idea six. The two named fallacies, which are really just the converse and the inverse wearing an argument's clothes.
Affirming the consequent. From if A, then B, and B is true, wrongly concluding A is true. That is the converse, treated as if it were guaranteed.

Claims example. If a loss is caused by flood, then it is excluded. The claim gets denied as excluded. Someone concludes, so it must have been flood. Wrong, because plenty of other things are also excluded under that same policy, wear and tear, earth movement, intentional acts. Being excluded does not pin the cause down to flood specifically.
Denying the antecedent. From if A, then B, and A is false, wrongly concluding B is false. That is the inverse, treated as if it were guaranteed.

Restoration example. If a roof is more than twenty years old, the carrier requires a four point inspection. This roof is twelve years old. Someone concludes, so no inspection required. Wrong, because the carrier might require that same inspection for a completely different reason, a prior claim on the file, a coastal wind zone, a specific roofing material the underwriter flags. The twenty year rule never spoke to any of that.

Both fallacies feel airtight in the moment, because there is a real, true conditional sitting right there in front of you. The mistake is always the same one. A promise that only ever ran one direction gets treated, without anyone noticing the swap, as if it ran both ways.
Time for the recap, fast, so you can hear which pieces you already have solid.

An argument is a conclusion plus its premises, and the conclusion is whatever the premises are trying to establish, not whatever sentence comes last. The assumption gap is whatever the conclusion depends on that nobody actually said, and naming it turns a vague feeling into a testable claim. A conditional, if A then B, promises nothing about the case where A is false. The contrapositive, if not B then not A, is the one guaranteed, automatic valid rewrite. The converse, if B then A, and the inverse, if not A then not B, are both invalid and can independently be true or false. Only if translates to if A then B, since it marks a necessary condition. Unless A, B translates to if not A then B. Necessary for B translates to if B then A. Sufficient for B translates to if A then B. Plain if B translates to if B then A, the reverse of only if. And affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are just the converse and the inverse smuggled into a two line argument.

Learn this chapter cold. Every scenario, every trap, every translation question in the rest of this track assumes you can already do every move I just walked you through, fast, without needing to pause and re-derive it. If any of the questions I asked gave you trouble, that is exactly where to drill before you move on.
